comments.content: restoreEnvVarReferences/restoreEnvVarsRecursive only match env vars by their full path. However, trackEnvVarMappings only records a mapping when the resolved value differs from the original (`value !== originalValue`). If a user sets a setting to a partial env var like `"prefix-${VAR}-suffix"`, trackEnvVarMappings will not record it because the regex requires the whole string to be an env var reference (`^\$(?:(\w+)|{([^}]+)})$`). As a result, such partially-interpolated values will be persisted with the resolved secret leaking into the file. Consider supporting embedded/partial env var references to avoid leaking secrets.

restoreEnvVarReferences guards existing values with `typeof value === 'string'` before restoring, but if an env-var-backed field's resolved value happens to be a non-string (e.g. a number resolved from an env var, or the mapping path now points at an object after an update), the original `$VAR` reference will NOT be restored and the resolved secret can leak. Since originalValue is always a string here, consider restoring regardless of the current value's type when the path matches a tracked mapping.

applyUpdates mutates `current` in place (`const result = current`) which is the object returned by comment-json's parse. This is generally fine here, but note that arrays in `updates` fully replace existing arrays rather than merging—verify this matches the merge semantics used elsewhere (customDeepMerge) so save/load round-trips are consistent.

When the file does not exist, this writes with plain JSON.stringify and ignores `envVarMappings`. If envVarMappings are provided but the file is newly created, resolved env var values could be written to disk. For consistency, apply restoreEnvVarReferences before writing here as well.
